summary: Scintillation is a free, public web tool that lets anyone look for things that move in the infrared sky. A user enters a sky position (RA and Dec). Scintillation gets NASA SPHEREx images of that patch from the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA), turns them all north-up, and plays them as a short “blink” animation. A nearby star, brown dwarf or asteroid then jumps from frame to frame. A difference view shows motion as a red-blue pair, and epoch stacks add frames together for deeper pictures. Scintillation also makes use of SPHEREx’s 102 wavelength bands. It plots a quick-look spectrum of the object at the centre and makes a false-colour picture. Optional ESA Gaia and WISE catalogue overlays identify known sources. Every view can be shared or embedded as a link. This simple tool lets students, amateur astronomers and the public explore that data and find candidates for scientists to check.
details:
What it does and how it works

  1. The user enters RA/Dec (degrees or hours/degrees), picks a quick target, or opens a shared link.
  2. Scintillation searches IRSA live for every SPHEREx image that covers that position.
  3. It reads each image’s wavelength from a very small “probe” cutout. Then it downloads full cutouts only for the frames it needs, in parallel and with a cache.
  4. Two modes build the animation:
    • Matched wavelength: a few frames at about the same wavelength, with an adjustable minimum date gap.
    • Epoch stacks: all frames from each observing period, added together per detector, for a deeper picture.
  5. Every frame is reprojected onto one north-up grid. The user can then watch the Blink, Step through frames with a slider, or Compare two frames or epochs. Compare shows the difference (red = brighter, blue = fainter) or the sum.
  6. Spectrum measures the centre object’s brightness in every frame, on the original pixels, and plots it against wavelength. The data can be downloaded as CSV. Colour shows short, middle and long wavelengths as blue, green and red.
  7. Optional Gaia DR3 and CatWISE2020 markers are moved to each frame’s date. The app shows details for the centre source, including WISE contamination flags. An object seen by WISE but not by Gaia is flagged as a potential cold brown dwarf.
  8. A watermarked demo mode uses synthetic data, so every feature works even when the archive is down.

Benefits and intended impact
SPHEREx data is public, but using it normally takes code and archive know-how. Scintillation takes this down to “type a position, watch it move”. Teachers can show proper motion and stellar spectra with real NASA data. Amateurs and citizen scientists can check targets and share links to interesting fields. Researchers get a quick-look viewer that can be embedded on other pages.

Tools and languages
Python 3.12 with Streamlit, Astropy, astroquery, reproject, PyVO, NumPy, pandas, Pillow and Vega-Altair. Data comes from NASA SPHEREx (DR1/QR3) through IRSA, using a method adapted from IRSA’s SPHEREx cutouts tutorial. Other data: ESA Gaia DR3, CatWISE2020 (WISE/NEOWISE) through NOIRLab Astro Data Lab, CDS Sesame/SIMBAD name lookup, and the NASA Exoplanet Archive. The app is hosted on Streamlit Community Cloud, and the code is on GitHub. AI tool: Claude (Anthropic), used for coding help, debugging and documentation. We made the design decisions and reviewed and tested all output.

What makes it creative

Scintillation animates the frames and uses SPHEREx’s 102 wavelength bands, so the same frames show both whether something moved and what it is, through a quick-look spectrum and a false-colour view. Gaia and WISE markers move with time to match each frame. The app flags objects that WISE sees but Gaia does not, which in this case is likely a sign of a cold brown dwarf. In a test the flag correctly picks out WISE 0855 as one. A plain-language glossary, shareable links and an always-working demo mode let anyone use it without any knowledge of astronomy archives.

What the team considered

There is some considerations about scientific accuracy...

  • Fast stars are moved to their 2026 positions. For example, Barnard’s Star is about 270″ from its catalogue position.
  • The app states that motion over six months is smaller than one SPHEREx pixel.
  • It warns when frames at different wavelengths are mixed.
  • It notes that pictures are for display, not measurement.

We want it to be publicly accessible. So we implemented WCAG contrast checks, a mobile layout, a readable font and a glossary in Simplified Technical English.

Open-source tools only, full references and licences in the README, AI use disclosed in the app, and no agency logos.

Current status
The catalogue features were checked on live data. For example, CatWISE finds WISE 0855 with a W1−W2 colour and motion that match published values. Because IRSA’s SPHEREx search service was overloaded during the hackathon, the image features were tested with the synthetic demo data.
